## Data for today

```{r size = "tiny"}
dat<-read_csv("https://www.openintro.org/data/csv/acs12.csv")
glimpse(dat)
```

## Subset the data to only include workers

```{r size = "tiny"}
dat <- dat |> 
  filter(employment == "employed")
```

## Let's look at income for this ACS 2012 sample

```{r fig.height = 4, size = "tiny"}
ggplot(dat,
       aes(x = income)) + 
  geom_histogram()
```

## Multiple regression (regression with more than 1 predictor)

We can generalize the linear regression 

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon$$
$$\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$$ \pause

as 

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 \cdots \beta_k x_k + \varepsilon$$
$$\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$$

Where $k$ is the number of predictor variables we include in the model. Our only constraint is that $k$ must be smaller than the number of observations $n$ in our data. 

## Multiple regression basics

1. Categorical predictors act as intercepts, or differences in level
2. Continuous predictors act as slopes

## Our model for income

Our theoretical model tells us that if we want to learn about $t \rightarrow i$, we must adjust for the effects that $e$ has on both $t$ and $i$. 

```{r}
m1 <- lm(income ~ hrs_work + edu,
         data = dat)
```

## Interpreting this model

```{r size = "tiny"}
table(dat$edu)
tidy(m1)
```

## To understand what the model says, let's visualize y-hat

```{r size = "tiny"}
# set up prediction data with values of interest
hrs_work<-0:60
edu<-c("college", "hs or lower", "grad")
pred_dat<-expand_grid(hrs_work, edu)
# generate expected values and CI, join pred_dat
e_y<-predict(m1, 
             newdata = pred_dat,
             interval = "confidence") |> 
  bind_cols(pred_dat)
# inspect
head(e_y)
```

## Visualizing model expectations

```{r fig.height = 4, size = "tiny"}
ggplot(e_y,
       aes(y = fit,
           ymin = lwr,
           ymax = upr,
           x = hrs_work,
           fill = edu,
           color = edu)) + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line() 
```

## Regression with more than one slope and multiple intercepts

Let's see if income depends on three variables: education, income, and hours worked

$$E(\textrm{income}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \textrm{hrs} + \beta_2 \textrm{edu} + \beta_3 \textrm{age}$$

## Fitting the model

```{r}
m2<-lm(income ~ hrs_work + 
         edu + 
         age,
       data = dat)

broom::tidy(m2)
```

## Visualizing model expectations: setup

```{r size = "tiny"}
# set up prediction data with values of interest
hrs_work<-0:40
age<-c(18:65)
edu<-c("college", "hs or lower", "grad")
pred_dat<-expand_grid(hrs_work, edu, age)
# generate expected values and CI, join pred_dat
e_y<-predict(m2, 
             newdata = pred_dat,
             interval = "confidence") |> 
  bind_cols(pred_dat)
# inspect
head(e_y)
```

## Visualizing model expectations: age and expected income

```{r echo = F}
ggplot(e_y |> 
         filter(hrs_work==40),
       aes(y = fit,
           ymin = lwr,
           ymax = upr,
           x = age,
           fill = edu,
           color = edu)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(subtitle = "Working 40 hours per week") + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, 120000))
```

## Hours worked and expected income

```{r echo = F}
ggplot(e_y |> 
         filter(age==40),
       aes(y = fit,
           ymin = lwr,
           ymax = upr,
           x = hrs_work,
           fill = edu,
           color = edu)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(subtitle = "Age 40")+ 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2) + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, 120000))
```

## Adding complexity: quadratic terms

We know that earnings for people less than age 18 and greater than age 70 tend to be very low (or zero). We can try to use a parabola (a quadratic equation) to model this process. 

Our revised model will be 

$$E(\textrm{income}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \textrm{hrs} + \beta_2 \textrm{edu} + \beta_3 \textrm{age} + \beta_4\textrm{age}^2$$

## Quadratics take a form that looks like this

```{r fig.height = 4}
pdat <- data.frame(x = -100:100)
p1 <- ggplot(pdat, aes(x = x, y = x^2)) + 
  geom_line() + labs(title = "y=x^2")
p2 <-  ggplot(pdat, aes(x = x, y = - x^2)) + 
  geom_line() + labs(title = "y=-x^2")
p1+p2
```

## Fitting a quadratic term

We use the I() function to require R to evaluate math statements inside formula objects

```{r}
m3<-lm(income ~ hrs_work + 
         edu +
         age + 
         I(age^2),
       data = dat)
tidy(m3)
```

## Visualizing model expectations

```{r echo = F}
# set up prediction data with values of interest
hrs_work<-40
age<-c(18:65)
edu<-c("college", "hs or lower", "grad")
pred_dat<-expand_grid(hrs_work, edu, age)
# generate expected values and CI, join pred_dat
e_y<-predict(m3, 
             newdata = pred_dat,
             interval = "confidence") |> 
  bind_cols(pred_dat)

ggplot(e_y,
       aes(y = fit,
           ymin = lwr,
           ymax = upr,
           x = age,
           fill = edu,
           color = edu)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(subtitle = "Working 40 hours per week")
```

## What about gender and education?

Perhaps we think that gender influences income. We can expand our model by including yet another predictor. 

```{r}
m4<-lm(income ~ -1 + # remove b0 to aid interpretation
         hrs_work + 
         edu +
         age + 
         gender,
       data = dat)
```

## What does this model say?

```{r}
summary(m4)
```

## Model expected values

```{r echo = F}
# set up prediction data with values of interest
hrs_work<-40
age<-c(18:65)
gender <- c("male", "female")
edu<-c("college", "hs or lower", "grad")
pred_dat<-expand_grid(hrs_work, edu, age, gender)
# generate expected values and CI, join pred_dat
e_y<-predict(m4, 
             newdata = pred_dat,
             interval = "confidence") |> 
  bind_cols(pred_dat) 

ggplot(e_y,
       aes(y = fit,
           ymin = lwr,
           ymax = upr,
           x = age,
           fill = gender,
           color = gender)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(subtitle = "Working 40 hours per week") + 
  facet_wrap(~edu)
```

## What if we think the impact of education on income depends on gender?

```{r echo = F}
gender_dag <- dagify(i~a+g+e,
                     e~a + g, 
                     outcome = "i", 
                     exposure = c("g", "e"))
ggdag(gender_dag) + theme_dag()
```

## Allowing the g->i relationship to vary by education

We can fit an *interaction* to the model to allow for separate parameters for all education and gender pairs

```{r}
m5<-lm(income ~ -1 + # remove b0 to aid interpretation
         hrs_work + 
         age + 
         edu * gender, # interaction
       data = dat)
```

## Interpreting model output: so many parameters!

```{r}
broom::tidy(m5)
```

## Visualizing the interaction

```{r echo = F}
# set up prediction data with values of interest
hrs_work<-40
age<-c(40)
gender <- c("male", "female")
edu<-c("college", "hs or lower", "grad")
pred_dat<-expand_grid(hrs_work, edu, age, gender)
# generate expected values and CI, join pred_dat
e_y<-predict(m5, 
             newdata = pred_dat,
             interval = "confidence") |> 
  bind_cols(pred_dat) 

ggplot(e_y,
       aes(y = fit,
           ymin = lwr,
           ymax = upr,
           x = edu,
           color = gender)) + 
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) + 
  labs(x = "education", y = "expected income")
```

## Categorical x categorical interactions

Interacting two categorical variables generates intercepts for each combination of levels of the two variables. Interacting a 2 level categorical with a 3 level categorical generates $2\times3=6$ intercepts.

## Categorical x continuous interactions

Let's allow the relation between age and income to vary by sex.

$$E(\textrm{income}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \textrm{hrs} + \beta_2 \textrm{edu} + \beta_3 \textrm{age} + \beta_4\textrm{gender} + \beta_5\textrm{gender x age}$$

## Fitting the model: interpretation is tricky

```{r}
m6<-lm(income ~ hrs_work + edu + 
         age * gender, # interaction
       data = dat)

broom::tidy(m6)
```

## But visualization makes it clear

```{r echo = F}
# set up fake data
pdat <- expand_grid(hrs_work = 40, edu = "college",
                    age=18:65, gender = c("male", "female")) 
# generate expected values with CI
yhat <- predict(m6, pdat, interval = "confidence")
# attach for plotting
pdat <- pdat |> bind_cols(yhat)
# plot
ggplot(pdat, aes(x = age, y = fit, ymin = lwr, 
                 ymax = upr, color = gender, fill = gender)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) 
```

## Categorical x continuous interactions

Interacting a categorical and a continuous variable generates different slopes for the continuous measure for each level of the categorical variable.

## Another example

Let's allow for differences in the slope of age by education

```{r}
m7<-lm(income ~ hrs_work + edu * age, # interaction
       data = dat)

broom::tidy(m7)
```

## Visualize

```{r echo = F}
# set up fake data
pdat <- expand_grid(hrs_work = 40, 
                    age=18:65, edu = unique(dat$edu)) 
# generate expected values with CI
yhat <- predict(m7, pdat, interval = "confidence")
# attach for plotting
pdat <- pdat |> bind_cols(yhat)
# plot
ggplot(pdat, aes(x = age, y = fit, ymin = lwr, 
                 ymax = upr, color = edu, fill = edu)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.5) 
```

## Continuous x continuous interactions

What if we think the effect of hours worked depends on age?

$$E(\textrm{income}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \textrm{hrs} + \beta_2 \textrm{age} + \beta_3 \textrm{age} \times \textrm{hrs}$$
```{r}
m8<-lm(income ~ hrs_work * age, # interaction
       data = dat)

broom::tidy(m8)
```

## Visualization

These are really tricky to interpret, you'll need to visualize it

```{r echo = F}
# set up fake data
pdat <- expand_grid(hrs_work = 10:60, 
                    age=c(18, 25, 35, 40, 50, 65)) 
# generate expected values with CI
yhat <- predict(m8, pdat, interval = "confidence")
# attach for plotting
pdat <- pdat |> bind_cols(yhat)
# plot
ggplot(pdat, aes(x = hrs_work, y = fit, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, color = -age, group = age)) + 
  geom_line() 
```

## Continuous x continuous interactions

Create constant changes in slope as both measures change. The allow for a very flexible model fit to the data, but are difficult to interpret directly.

## Combining interactions

Sometimes it makes sense to *fully* interact your model, allow each measure to interact with all other measures. Let's see this with age, hrs_work, and education

```{r}
m9<-lm(income ~ hrs_work * age * edu, # interaction
       data = dat)
broom::tidy(m9)
```

## Visualization

What looks off here?

```{r echo = F}
# set up fake data
pdat <- expand_grid(hrs_work = 10:60, 
                    age=c(18, 40, 65), edu = unique(dat$edu)) 
# generate expected values with CI
yhat <- predict(m9, pdat, interval = "confidence")
# attach for plotting
pdat <- pdat |> bind_cols(yhat)
# plot
ggplot(pdat, aes(x = hrs_work, y = fit, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr,
                 color = edu, fill = edu)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.2, color = NULL) + 
  facet_wrap(~age)
```
